title: Ethos: The Speaker’s Character
short: Ethos persuades through the character the speaker shows: good sense, good character and goodwill toward the audience.
trouble: Learners think ethos means quoting an expert. For Aristotle it is the trust the speech itself earns; a writer builds it with fairness, knowledge and respect for the reader.

blocks.html: Aristotle named three kinds of proof that a speech itself can supply: the speaker’s character (ethos), the audience’s frame of mind (pathos), and the argument (logos). This topic starts with ethos, the writer corner of the rhetorical situation.

We believe people we trust, especially on questions where certainty isn’t possible. In Book II of the Rhetoric, Aristotle says listeners trust a speaker who shows three things: good sense (practical wisdom), good character (honesty and virtue), and goodwill toward the audience. And he means the character shown in the speech, not only a reputation brought to it.

fill.writer: shows good sense, character and goodwill

blocks.cap: Ethos lives in the writer corner: the trust the text earns.

blocks.html: Ethos persuades through the character a writer shows: good sense, good character and goodwill. A writer earns it on the page with accuracy, fairness, knowledge and respect for the reader.

Readers can’t check everything themselves. When they decide whether to believe a claim, they also decide whether to believe the person making it. A writer who is fair to the other side, admits limits and gets small facts right gives readers a reason to trust the big claims too.

head: Quality
How a writer shows it
rows: accurate facts, sensible plans, knowing the subject, admitting what is uncertain
honesty, fairness to opponents, owning mistakes, no tricks
respect for the audience, care for their interests, a reasonable tone
blocks.cap: Aristotle’s three sources of trust, in practice.

blocks.title: Ethos in the Federalist
blocks.q: In Federalist No. 1 (1787), Hamilton writes that we “see wise and good men on the wrong as well as on the right side of questions of the first magnitude to society.” He also says: “My arguments will be open to all, and may be judged of by all.” How do these sentences build ethos?
steps: Hamilton is arguing for the new Constitution, but he grants that good people disagree with him. That is fairness: good character.
He invites readers to judge his reasons, not his motives. That shows confidence in his case and respect for the reader: goodwill.
Readers who feel respected are more willing to listen to what comes next.
blocks.a: He earns trust by treating opponents fairly and inviting readers to judge his arguments themselves.

blocks.title: Ethos through modesty
blocks.q: Douglass opened his Fourth of July oration: “He who could address this audience without a quailing sensation, has stronger nerves than I have.” Why begin a powerful speech by sounding nervous?
steps: A modest opening was a common way to win an audience’s goodwill: the speaker seems humble, not arrogant.
It also reminds listeners of the distance he has traveled; a few lines later he speaks of “the slave plantation, from which I escaped.”
The humble start makes the fierce passages later in the speech hit harder.
blocks.a: The modest opening builds goodwill and character before the speech turns forceful.

blocks.html: Thinking ethos just means quoting an expert or listing credentials. Credentials help, and citing an expert is often wise, but Aristotle’s ethos is the trust the writing itself earns. A famous name can’t rescue a sloppy, unfair essay, and an unknown student can earn trust with careful facts and a fair tone. Check: would a reader who knew nothing about you trust you after reading this paragraph?

blocks.name: wr-mark

sentences.text: I have run the school’s recycling club for two years, so I have seen what fills our bins.
I’ll admit my first plan, a ban on plastic bottles, would have been unfair to students without reusable ones.
I know the custodians already work hard, so this plan adds no work for them.
Last month we sorted 40 bags of recycling, and 12 of them were mostly trash.

blocks.cap: Four sentences from a student’s proposal, each building a different kind of trust.
